# Part III: Post-Training: Adaptation, Preference, and Alignment {#part-adaptation .unnumbered}

> "Making language models bigger does not inherently make them better at
> following a user's intent."
>
> Long Ouyang et al., ["Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)

Part I produced a base model that learns the shape of text; Part II followed the
generative and multimodal architectures that branch off the same foundations.
This part returns to that base model and the gap it leaves: it does not yet know
which behavior a product wants from it, which refusal a policy requires, which
authority to obey in a conflict, or which answer a human will prefer. The weights
already contain a great deal of capability, but capability by itself is not a
usable interface. It must be pointed, constrained, ranked, tested, and sometimes
taught to prefer one kind of answer over another.

@sec-sft-peft starts with the most direct intervention: demonstrations that
reshape behavior, often through small adapters rather than a full rewrite of the
model. @sec-behavior-specs then asks what the preference signal is supposed to
mean, tracing behavior specifications, constitutions, annotator protocols, and
multi-attribute preference data before any optimizer sees them. @sec-rlhf
introduces the reward-modeling loop, where the system learns from comparisons
and a reward proxy rather than from a single correct answer. @sec-dpo-variants
shows why that loop can be algebraically folded into direct preference
objectives, and why the many variants differ less by slogan than by the balances
they choose. @sec-verifiable-rewards separates learned rewards from checkable
ones, the hinge that connects this part to the reasoning machinery in
@sec-training-to-reason. @sec-safety-tuning follows the same post-training stack
into refusals, instruction hierarchy, and deliberation over written policy.
@sec-synthetic-data closes the circle by letting models produce, filter, judge,
and improve on data that no longer came directly from a human labeler.

As this part proceeds, the word alignment narrows. It does not mean making a
model good in every sense. It means choosing a training signal, accepting its
proxy failures, and deciding where oversight enters the loop. The central cost
is no longer only compute. It is trust in the signal that tells the model what
better means.
